---
title: "Medicare at 65: Sharp RD Identification"
subtitle: "Checking the continuity assumption before estimating the effect"
knit: |
  (function(inputFile, ...) {
    candidates <- c(
      file.path(Sys.getenv('LOCALAPPDATA'), 'Programs', 'Pandoc'),
      file.path(Sys.getenv('LOCALAPPDATA'), 'Pandoc'),
      file.path(Sys.getenv('ProgramFiles'), 'Pandoc'),
      file.path(Sys.getenv('ProgramFiles'), 'RStudio', 'resources',
                'app', 'bin', 'quarto', 'bin', 'tools')
    )
    found <- candidates[file.exists(file.path(candidates, 'pandoc.exe'))]
    if (length(found)) Sys.setenv(RSTUDIO_PANDOC = found[1])
    project <- dirname(normalizePath(inputFile, winslash = '/', mustWork = TRUE))
    while (!file.exists(file.path(project, 'data', 'nhis_clean_full.csv'))) {
      parent <- dirname(project)
      if (identical(parent, project)) stop('Cannot locate project data.')
      project <- parent
    }
    destination <- file.path(project, 'output', 'sharp_rd_identification')
    dir.create(destination, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    options <- list(...)
    options$output_dir <- destination
    options$intermediates_dir <- tempdir()
    do.call(rmarkdown::render, c(list(input = inputFile), options))
  })
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_float: true
    toc_depth: 2
    number_sections: true
    theme: flatly
    highlight: tango
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE,message=FALSE,error=FALSE,
                      fig.width=9,fig.height=5,dpi=160,fig.align='center')
source('rd_functions.R')
root <- find_root()
out <- file.path(root,'output','sharp_rd_identification')
dir.create(out,recursive=TRUE,showWarnings=FALSE)
d <- load_rd_data(root)
H <- 5; H_alt <- c(3,4,5,6,7)
win <- subset(d,abs(age4-65)<H)
balance_vars <- c('female','wnh','bnh','hispanic','lowed_clean','region_1','region_2','region_3')
stopifnot(all(vapply(d[c(balance_vars,'emp','mcare','sawdr','inhosp')],
                     function(v) all(na.omit(v) %in% 0:1),logical(1))))
wmean <- function(v,w) {ok <- !is.na(v); weighted.mean(v[ok],w[ok])}
pv <- function(p) format.pval(p,digits=3,eps=.001)
ci <- function(r) sprintf('[%s, %s]',pct(r$ci_lower),pct(r$ci_upper))
```

# Research design and identifying assumption

## Question and estimand

We ask how becoming eligible for Medicare at 65 changes healthcare use in the United States. The sharp RD estimand is the gap in expected outcomes just above and just below the cutoff:

$$\tau_{RD}=\lim_{a\downarrow 65}E[Y_i\mid Age_i=a]-\lim_{a\uparrow 65}E[Y_i\mid Age_i=a].$$

Treatment is **eligibility**, $D_i=1(Age_i\ge65)$, not Medicare coverage. $\tau_{RD}$ is therefore an intention-to-treat effect of eligibility for people near 65. The main outcome is seeing a doctor in the past year (`sawdr`); an overnight hospital stay (`inhosp`) is secondary. Self-rated health is not used, because Medicare can change it.

This report checks the design only. **It does not estimate the jump in either outcome at 65.** Those estimates and their robustness checks are in `sharp_rd_estimation.Rmd`.

## The identifying assumption

<div class="finding">

**Continuity.** $E[Y_i(0)\mid Age_i=a]$ and $E[Y_i(1)\mid Age_i=a]$ are continuous at $a=65$ (Hahn, Todd and van der Klaauw, 2001; Card, Dobkin and Maestas, 2008).

In words: without the Medicare rule, healthcare use would change smoothly as people pass 65. If anything else jumps at 65, or the people just above 65 differ from those just below, the jump in $Y$ is not Medicare's effect.

</div>

Continuity involves potential outcomes, so it cannot be tested directly. We test what it implies: characteristics that are fixed before 65 should be smooth through the cutoff, nobody should be sorted across it, and no other determinant of healthcare use should jump there.

## Why the assumption is plausible

- **Age cannot be manipulated.** Unlike test scores or income, nobody can choose which side of 65 they are on.
- **Local comparability.** People on either side of the cutoff differ in age by a few months.
- **Eligibility is a strict function of age.** Medicare eligibility begins at 65 for nearly everyone with a work history, so the rule itself does not create selection.

## What "sharp" means in this data

Age (`age4`) is measured in quarter-years: $(4\times(\text{interview year}-\text{birth year})+\text{interview quarter}-\text{birth quarter})/4$. Eligibility `post65` is exactly $1(age4\ge65)$:

```{r sharp-check}
stopifnot(all(d$post65==as.integer(d$age4>=65)))
cells <- subset(d,age4>=64 & age4<=66)
sharp <- do.call(rbind,lapply(split(cells,cells$age4),function(v) data.frame(
  Age=sprintf('%.2f',v$age4[1]),Respondents=format(nrow(v),big.mark=','),
  `Coded eligible`=sprintf('%.0f%%',100*mean(v$post65)),
  `Medicare coverage`=sprintf('%.1f%%',100*wmean(v$mcare,v$wt)),check.names=FALSE)))
knitr::kable(sharp,align='rrrr',row.names=FALSE)
```

<div class="caution">

Two features of the data make the cutoff less than perfectly sharp. Both are handled in the estimation report.

1. **The 65.00 cell is only partly treated.** A respondent coded 65.00 was interviewed in their birth quarter, so their true age lies between about 64.75 and 65.25. Roughly half have not turned 65 yet, which is why Medicare coverage in that cell (`r sharp[sharp$Age=='65.00','Medicare coverage']`) sits between the cells either side. Cells 64.75 and below are fully below the cutoff, and 65.25 and above are fully above it. The estimation report runs a donut RD that drops this cell. Coverage also rises in the cells just below 65, probably because Medicare starts on the first day of the birth month and because of reporting error in quarter-based age.
2. **The outcomes look back 12 months.** `sawdr` and `inhosp` refer to the past year, so someone aged 65.25 has had at most three months of eligibility inside the recall window. The effect should build up between 65 and 66 rather than appear as a clean step. This makes the RD estimate a conservative (attenuated) measure of the effect.

</div>

## Threats to identification and how we check them

| Threat | Why it matters | Check |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Different people on each side of 65 | The jump in $Y$ could reflect who they are rather than Medicare | Section 3: covariate balance and a joint covariate index |
| Sorting or heaping in age | Rounding or misreporting could pile respondents onto one side | Section 2: histogram by age quarter |
| Retirement at 65 (Social Security full retirement age) | Retirement changes income, free time and employer insurance, and could raise doctor visits on its own | Section 4: employment RD, falsification tests, positive control at 62 and a bias bound |
| Something other than Medicare drives the jump | Attribution to Medicare needs a pattern only Medicare explains | Section 5: subgroup coverage and employment jumps, with a stated prediction |
| Delaying care until 65, or a partly treated cell | Creates a dip below 65 or blurs the jump | Estimation report: donut RD and placebo cutoffs on the outcomes |
| Employer coverage becoming secondary to Medicare | Happens *because of* Medicare | Part of the treatment, not a confounder |

## Specification used for every check

All checks use local linear regression within **`r H` years of 65**, with separate age slopes on each side, survey-year fixed effects, NHIS survey weights and a triangular kernel. Alternative bandwidths of `r paste(setdiff(H_alt,H),collapse=', ')` years are reported. The bandwidth is fixed in years rather than chosen by a data-driven rule, because quarterly age gives few distinct values near the cutoff and data-driven selectors can behave badly with so few mass points. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1).

$$Y_i=\alpha+\tau\,1(Age_i\ge65)+\beta(Age_i-65)+\delta\,1(Age_i\ge65)(Age_i-65)+\lambda_{year(i)}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad |Age_i-65|<h.$$

Each jump is reported in percentage points and relative to the fitted rate just below 65.

## Data and sample

```{r sample}
miss_vars <- c('sawdr','inhosp','emp','mcare','female','wnh','bnh','hispanic','lowed_clean','region')
miss <- data.frame(Variable=miss_vars,
  `Missing below 65`=sapply(miss_vars,function(v) sprintf('%.1f%%',100*mean(is.na(win[[v]][win$age4<65])))),
  `Missing 65 and above`=sapply(miss_vars,function(v) sprintf('%.1f%%',100*mean(is.na(win[[v]][win$age4>=65])))),
  check.names=FALSE)
```

The analysis sample has **`r format(nrow(d),big.mark=',')` respondents from NHIS `r min(d$year)`-`r max(d$year)`**, aged `r min(d$age4)`-`r max(d$age4)`, with `r length(unique(d$age4))` distinct quarter-age values. Of these, `r format(nrow(win),big.mark=',')` are within `r H` years of 65. The cleaned file covers 1992-1996 only, not the 1992-2003 period in the proposal, so it avoids the 1997 NHIS redesign; survey-year fixed effects absorb any remaining changes across years. Respondents with a missing doctor-visit outcome were removed upstream. Other missing values are dropped separately for each test.

```{r sample-table, results='asis'}
cat(knitr::kable(miss,align='lrr',row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

Missingness is low and similar on both sides of 65. The main exception is Medicare coverage, which is used only in Section 5.

# Check 1: no sorting or heaping in age

```{r heaping}
counts <- table(d$age4)
near <- counts[names(counts) %in% c('64.5','64.75','65.25','65.5')]
ratio65 <- as.numeric(counts['65'])/mean(near)
integer_share <- mean(d$age4==round(d$age4))
heap_pass <- abs(ratio65-1)<.1 & abs(integer_share-.25)<.02
```

```{r age-histogram, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap='Respondents by quarter-year of age. The dashed line marks age 65.'}
hist(d$age4,breaks=seq(55,75,by=.25),right=FALSE,
     main='Age distribution by quarter-year',xlab='Age',ylab='Respondents',
     col='#8ca8b7',border='white',col.main='#17465c')
abline(v=65,lty=2,col='#B2182B',lwd=2)
```

<div class="finding">

Respondents are spread evenly across age quarters. The 65.00 cell has `r format(counts['65'],big.mark=',')` respondents, `r sprintf('%.2f',ratio65)` times the average of the two cells on either side. Whole-year ages make up `r sprintf('%.1f%%',100*integer_share)` of the sample, against 25% if there were no rounding to whole years. `r if(heap_pass) 'There is no sign of heaping at 65 or of rounding to whole years.' else 'The counts deviate from an even spread and should be investigated before estimation.'` Because nobody can choose their age, any bunching would have pointed to survey reporting problems rather than manipulation.

</div>

# Check 2: covariate balance

If people just above 65 are the same kind of people as those just below, characteristics fixed before 65 should not jump at the cutoff. We test sex, race/ethnicity, below-high-school education and region. One category from each exhaustive set is omitted (other non-Hispanic race; West).

```{r balance-fit}
balance <- rd_rows(lapply(balance_vars,function(y) fit_rd(d,y,H)))
balance$p_holm <- p.adjust(balance$p_value,'holm')
balance_h <- rd_rows(unlist(lapply(balance_vars,function(y) lapply(H_alt,function(h) fit_rd(d,y,h))),recursive=FALSE))
```

## Binned plots

```{r balance-plots, fig.height=11, fig.cap='Covariates against age using the main five-year bandwidth. Points are weighted quarter-age means; lines are local linear fits on each side of 65.'}
par(mfrow=c(4,2),mar=c(4,4.5,3,1),cex=.9)
for(y in balance_vars) plot_rd(d,y,H)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

## RD estimates

```{r balance-table, results='asis'}
cat(table_rd(balance,unname(rd_labels[balance$outcome])),sep='\n')
```

Of the `r nrow(balance)` tests, `r sum(balance$p_value<.05)` reject zero at 5% before adjusting for multiple tests and `r sum(balance$p_holm<.05)` after the Holm adjustment.

## Bandwidth sensitivity

Jumps in percentage points, with p-values in brackets.

```{r balance-bandwidth, results='asis'}
bh <- reshape(transform(balance_h[,c('outcome','bandwidth')],
                        cell=sprintf('%s (%s)',pct(balance_h$estimate),pv(balance_h$p_value))),
              idvar='outcome',timevar='bandwidth',direction='wide')
names(bh) <- c('Covariate',paste0('+/-',H_alt,' years'))
bh$Covariate <- unname(rd_labels[bh$Covariate])
cat(knitr::kable(bh,align=c('l',rep('r',length(H_alt))),row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

## Joint test: covariate index

Separate tests can each miss small imbalances that add up. To combine them, we regress each outcome on all covariates (sex, race/ethnicity, education, region), **using only respondents below 65**, and predict it for everyone. If the covariates are balanced overall, this predicted outcome should not jump at 65. The prediction weights each covariate by how strongly it relates to healthcare use, so the test focuses on the imbalances that would matter. Fitting only below 65 means no post-eligibility outcomes are used, and no jump in the actual outcome is estimated.

```{r index}
index_formula <- ~female+bnh+hispanic+onh+lowed_clean+factor(region)
for(y in c('sawdr','inhosp')) {
  m <- lm(update(index_formula,as.formula(paste(y,'~.'))),data=subset(d,age4<65),weights=wt)
  d[[paste0(y,'_index')]] <- predict(m,newdata=d)
}
rd_labels['inhosp_index'] <- 'Predicted hospital stay (covariate index)'
index <- rd_rows(lapply(c('sawdr_index','inhosp_index'),function(y) fit_rd(d,y,H)))
index_pass <- all(index$p_value>=.05)
```

```{r index-table, results='asis'}
cat(table_rd(index,unname(rd_labels[index$outcome])),sep='\n')
```

```{r index-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap='Outcomes predicted from covariates alone. A jump would mean the mix of people changes at 65 in a way that matters for healthcare use.'}
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,4.5,3,1))
plot_rd(d,'sawdr_index',H,main='Predicted doctor visit')
plot_rd(d,'inhosp_index',H,main='Predicted hospital stay')
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

<div class="finding">

`r if(sum(balance$p_holm<.05)==0) 'No covariate jumps significantly at 65 after adjusting for multiple tests.' else paste('Some covariates jump significantly at 65 after adjustment:',paste(rd_labels[balance$outcome[balance$p_holm<.05]],collapse=', '),'. These need to be controlled for and discussed.')` The covariate index for doctor visits changes by `r pct(index$estimate[1],2)` pp at 65 (p = `r pv(index$p_value[1])`), and the index for hospital stays by `r pct(index$estimate[2],2)` pp (p = `r pv(index$p_value[2])`). `r if(index_pass) 'Based on observed characteristics, the people on either side of 65 look comparable in the ways that matter for healthcare use.' else 'The combined covariates shift at 65, so the outcome estimates should be reported with and without covariate controls.'` Insignificant jumps are consistent with balance but do not prove it, and these tests cannot say anything about unobserved characteristics.

</div>

# Check 3: retirement and other changes at 65

During 1992-1996, 65 was the Social Security full retirement age. If many people stopped working at 65, retirement could raise doctor visits on its own (more free time, a change in income or insurance), and the age-65 jump would mix Medicare and retirement. Retirement caused *by* Medicare is part of the eligibility effect; the concern is retirement driven by other age-65 incentives. Employment is the direct check.

```{r employment-fit}
employment <- rd_rows(lapply(H_alt,function(h) fit_rd(d,'emp',h)))
e <- employment[employment$bandwidth==H,]
falsify <- rd_rows(list(fit_rd(d,'emp',H,donut=.25),fit_rd(d,'emp',2,60),fit_rd(d,'emp',2,70)))
control62 <- fit_rd(d,'emp',2,62)
c62 <- control62$row
emp_pass <- e$p_value>=.05
```

## Employment at 65

```{r employment-plot, fig.cap='Employment around age 65. Points are weighted quarter-age means; lines are local linear fits.'}
plot_rd(d,'emp',H)
```

```{r employment-table, results='asis'}
cat(table_rd(employment,paste0('+/-',employment$bandwidth,' years')),sep='\n')
```

<div class="finding">

The employment jump at 65 is **`r pct(e$estimate)` percentage points** (95% CI `r ci(e)`; p = `r pv(e$p_value)`), against a fitted employment rate of `r pct(e$below_rate,1)`% just below 65. That is a relative change of `r pct(e$relative,1)`%. `r if(emp_pass) paste0('There is no significant employment change at 65, and the confidence interval rules out an employment drop larger than ', pct(max(0,-e$ci_lower)), ' pp.') else 'Employment changes significantly at 65, so retirement is a live competing explanation and the bias bound below is central to the interpretation.'` The result is `r if(all(employment$p_value>=.05)) 'insignificant at every bandwidth from 3 to 7 years' else 'not stable across bandwidths; see the table'`.

</div>

## Falsification tests

The donut drops the partly treated 65.00 cell. The placebo cutoffs at 60 and 70 use two-year windows, which keep each window clear of both 62 and 65.

```{r falsify-table, results='asis'}
cat(table_rd(falsify,c('Donut: drop the 65.00 cell (+/-5 years)',
                       'Placebo at 60 (+/-2 years)','Placebo at 70 (+/-2 years)')),sep='\n')
```

## Positive control: age 62

The placebos show the test does not find jumps where none should exist. They do not show it *can* find a real one. Age 62 is the earliest age for claiming Social Security, and many people retire then, so an employment drop is expected there. Finding a drop at 62 but not at 65 shows the method can detect retirement discontinuities and that one is absent at 65.

```{r control62-plot, fig.cap='Employment around age 62 (two-year window), where early Social Security claiming begins.'}
plot_rd(d,'emp',2,62,main='Employment around 62',fit=control62)
```

```{r control62-table, results='asis'}
cat(table_rd(c62,'Positive control at 62 (+/-2 years)'),sep='\n')
```

<div class="finding">

At 62, employment changes by **`r pct(c62$estimate)` pp** (95% CI `r ci(c62)`; p = `r pv(c62$p_value)`). `r if(c62$p_value<.05 && c62$estimate<0) 'The test detects the expected retirement drop at 62, so the absence of a drop at 65 is informative.' else 'The test does not detect a significant drop at 62 either, so it may lack the power to detect retirement discontinuities of this size. The insignificant employment result at 65 should therefore be read with caution.'`

</div>

## How much bias could retirement cause?

An insignificant estimate does not mean zero. To put an upper limit on the bias, take the largest employment drop the confidence interval allows and multiply it by the gap in healthcare use between people who are not working and people who are, measured among respondents aged 60-64.75:

$$\text{max bias} = \underbrace{\max(0,-\text{CI}_{lower})}_{\text{largest plausible employment drop}}\times\underbrace{(\bar Y_{\text{not employed}}-\bar Y_{\text{employed}})}_{\text{gap below 65}}.$$

This is a descriptive comparison below the cutoff, not an RD estimate. It overstates the causal effect of retirement, because people out of work tend to be in worse health, which makes the bound conservative.

```{r bias-bound}
pre <- subset(d,age4>=60 & age4<65)
drop_max <- max(0,-e$ci_lower)
bound <- do.call(rbind,lapply(c('sawdr','inhosp'),function(y) {
  ok <- !is.na(pre[[y]]) & !is.na(pre$emp)
  gap <- wmean(pre[[y]][ok & pre$emp==0],pre$wt[ok & pre$emp==0])-
         wmean(pre[[y]][ok & pre$emp==1],pre$wt[ok & pre$emp==1])
  data.frame(outcome=y,emp_drop_max=drop_max,gap=gap,max_bias=drop_max*abs(gap))
}))
```

```{r bias-table, results='asis'}
cat(knitr::kable(data.frame(Outcome=unname(rd_labels[bound$outcome]),
  `Largest employment drop (pp)`=pct(bound$emp_drop_max),
  `Gap: not employed minus employed (pp)`=pct(bound$gap),
  `Maximum retirement bias (pp)`=pct(bound$max_bias),check.names=FALSE),
  align='lrrr',row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

<div class="finding">

Even under these conservative assumptions, retirement could account for at most **`r pct(bound$max_bias[1])` pp** of any jump in doctor visits at 65 and **`r pct(bound$max_bias[2])` pp** of any jump in hospital stays. The estimation report compares these bounds with the estimated jumps.

</div>

# Check 4: subgroup pattern

The employment RD tests retirement directly. The subgroup pattern gives a second, independent test of attribution. If Medicare drives the jump in healthcare use, groups whose Medicare coverage jumps more at 65 should show larger jumps in use. If retirement drove it, the jumps in use should instead follow the jumps in employment. We use the four race × education groups (`group`) and Medicare coverage (`mcare`), the project's first-stage variable.

This section estimates only the coverage and employment jumps by group, and states the prediction **before** the outcome jumps are estimated. The estimation report tests it.

```{r subgroups}
sub <- do.call(rbind,lapply(1:4,function(g) {
  dg <- subset(d,group==g); pg <- subset(dg,age4>=60 & age4<65)
  m <- fit_rd(dg,'mcare',H)$row; w <- fit_rd(dg,'emp',H)$row
  data.frame(group=g,label=group_labels[[as.character(g)]],
    n=sum(abs(dg$age4-65)<H),
    pre_mcare=wmean(pg$mcare,pg$wt),pre_uninsured=1-wmean(pg$covered2,pg$wt),
    mcare_jump=m$estimate,mcare_lo=m$ci_lower,mcare_hi=m$ci_upper,mcare_p=m$p_value,
    emp_jump=w$estimate,emp_lo=w$ci_lower,emp_hi=w$ci_upper,emp_p=w$p_value)
}))
sub$mcare_rank <- rank(-sub$mcare_jump)
sub$emp_rank <- rank(sub$emp_jump)
predicted <- sub$label[order(sub$mcare_rank)]
```

```{r subgroup-table, results='asis'}
cat(knitr::kable(data.frame(Group=sub$label,N=format(sub$n,big.mark=','),
  `Medicare before 65`=paste0(pct(sub$pre_mcare,1),'%'),
  `Uninsured before 65`=paste0(pct(sub$pre_uninsured,1),'%'),
  `Medicare jump (pp)`=sprintf('%s [%s, %s]',pct(sub$mcare_jump,1),pct(sub$mcare_lo,1),pct(sub$mcare_hi,1)),
  `Employment jump (pp)`=sprintf('%s [%s, %s]',pct(sub$emp_jump,1),pct(sub$emp_lo,1),pct(sub$emp_hi,1)),
  check.names=FALSE),align='lrrrrr',row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

Rates before 65 are weighted means for ages 60-64.75. The uninsured rate is descriptive context only; it is not a first-stage variable.

```{r subgroup-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap='Jumps at 65 by race and education group, with 95% confidence intervals.'}
dot <- function(est,lo,hi,main,col) {
  yy <- 4:1
  plot(100*est,yy,xlim=range(0,100*c(lo,hi)),ylim=c(.5,4.5),yaxt='n',pch=19,col=col,
       xlab='Jump at 65 (pp)',ylab='',main=main,bty='l',col.main='#17465c',col.axis='#637783')
  abline(v=0,lty=2,col='#82949f')
  segments(100*lo,yy,100*hi,yy,col=col,lwd=2)
  axis(2,at=yy,labels=sub$label,las=1,cex.axis=.85,col.axis='#344f60')
}
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,13,3,1))
dot(sub$mcare_jump,sub$mcare_lo,sub$mcare_hi,'Medicare coverage','#176d85')
dot(sub$emp_jump,sub$emp_lo,sub$emp_hi,'Employment','#c17948')
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

<div class="finding">

**Prediction for the estimation report.** If Medicare drives the effect, the jumps in doctor visits and hospital stays should be largest for **`r predicted[1]`** and smallest for **`r predicted[4]`**, following the Medicare coverage jumps (`r paste(predicted,collapse=' > ')`). `r if(all(sub$emp_p>=.05)) 'No group shows a significant employment jump at 65, so retirement offers no competing reason for the outcome jumps to differ across groups.' else paste0('Employment jumps significantly for: ', paste(sub$label[sub$emp_p<.05],collapse=', '), '. If outcome jumps follow the employment ranking rather than the coverage ranking, retirement is the more likely explanation.')`

</div>

```{r uninsured-order}
uninsured_order <- sub$label[order(-sub$pre_uninsured)]
```

<div class="caution">

**Reading the prediction.** Medicare coverage jumps include people *switching* from other insurance, not only people *gaining* insurance. Ranked by the share uninsured before 65, the order is `r paste(uninsured_order,collapse=' > ')`, `r if(identical(uninsured_order,rev(predicted))) 'the exact reverse of' else 'different from'` the Medicare-jump order. The two orders separate two channels. If outcome jumps follow the Medicare order, the effect works through Medicare coverage generally, including more generous coverage for people who were already insured. If they follow the uninsured order, it works mainly through newly gaining insurance. Either way, a pattern that follows employment instead would point to retirement. Confidence intervals for the Medicare jumps overlap for some groups, so only clear differences between groups should be interpreted.

</div>

# Summary

## Scorecard

```{r scorecard, results='asis'}
score <- data.frame(
  Check=c('Heaping in age','Covariate balance','Covariate index','Employment at 65',
          'Employment falsification','Positive control at 62','Subgroup pattern'),
  `What it tests`=c('Sorting or rounding of age around 65','Comparable people on each side',
                    'Combined imbalance relevant to healthcare use','Retirement at 65',
                    'Donut and placebo cutoffs for employment','Whether the employment test can detect retirement',
                    'Attribution to Medicare'),
  Result=c(sprintf('65.00 cell is %.2f times its neighbours; %.1f%% whole-year ages',ratio65,100*integer_share),
           sprintf('%d of %d significant after Holm',sum(balance$p_holm<.05),nrow(balance)),
           sprintf('Doctor visits %s pp (p = %s); hospital %s pp (p = %s)',pct(index$estimate[1]),pv(index$p_value[1]),pct(index$estimate[2]),pv(index$p_value[2])),
           sprintf('%s pp, CI %s, p = %s; max bias %s pp',pct(e$estimate),ci(e),pv(e$p_value),pct(bound$max_bias[1])),
           sprintf('%d of 3 significant',sum(falsify$p_value<.05)),
           sprintf('%s pp, p = %s',pct(c62$estimate),pv(c62$p_value)),
           paste('Predicted order:',paste(predicted,collapse=' > '))),
  Verdict=c(ifelse(heap_pass,'Pass','Investigate'),
            ifelse(all(balance$p_holm>=.05),'Pass','Investigate'),
            ifelse(index_pass,'Pass','Investigate'),
            ifelse(emp_pass,'Pass','Concern'),
            ifelse(all(falsify$p_value>=.05),'Pass','Investigate'),
            ifelse(c62$p_value<.05 && c62$estimate<0,'Drop detected','Low power'),
            'Tested in estimation report'),
  check.names=FALSE)
cat(knitr::kable(score,align='llll',row.names=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

## What remains assumed

These checks support continuity but cannot prove it. Three things remain assumptions:

- **Unobserved characteristics are smooth at 65.** Balance in sex, race, education and region does not guarantee balance in, for example, health status or income.
- **Small retirement effects.** The employment confidence interval does not rule out small changes. The bias bound limits how much they could matter.
- **Selection into the doctor-visit sample.** Respondents with a missing doctor-visit answer were removed before this analysis, so we cannot test whether that missingness changes at 65.

## What the estimation report needs from this one

- **Specification:** local linear, `r H`-year main bandwidth, alternatives of `r paste(setdiff(H_alt,H),collapse=', ')` years, triangular kernel, survey-year fixed effects, survey weights, HC1 standard errors (shared through `rd_functions.R`).
- **Retirement bias bounds:** `r pct(bound$max_bias[1])` pp for doctor visits and `r pct(bound$max_bias[2])` pp for hospital stays.
- **Subgroup prediction:** outcome jumps should follow the Medicare coverage order `r paste(predicted,collapse=' > ')`.
- **Donut RD:** drop the partly treated 65.00 cell. A wider donut (64.75-65.25) addresses people delaying care until 65. The 12-month recall window means the estimate is likely attenuated.

```{r export}
export <- rbind(
  transform(balance,check='covariate balance'),
  transform(balance_h,check='covariate balance by bandwidth',p_holm=NA_real_),
  transform(index,check='covariate index',p_holm=NA_real_),
  transform(employment,check='employment',p_holm=NA_real_),
  transform(falsify,check=c('employment donut','employment placebo','employment placebo'),p_holm=NA_real_),
  transform(c62,check='employment positive control',p_holm=NA_real_))
write.csv(export,file.path(out,'identification_results.csv'),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(bound,file.path(out,'handoff_bias_bound.csv'),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(sub,file.path(out,'handoff_subgroups.csv'),row.names=FALSE)
```
